passages.title: Air Travel vs. the Environment
passages.subtitle: Confronting budget aviation, rail alternatives, and the limits of carbon offsets
paragraphs: The deregulation of aviation and the emergence of budget airlines transformed air travel from an elite privilege into an everyday habit. Discount carriers opened regional airports across Europe and Asia, allowing students, migrant workers, and families to enjoy unprecedented travel freedom at prices that frequently undercut long-distance train tickets.

From a climate standpoint, however, cheap flights carry an outsized toll. Per passenger kilometre, short-haul jets emit several times more carbon emissions than high-speed rail and significantly more than a shared petrol car. Worse still, aircraft release nitrogen oxides and water vapour at cruising altitude, forming condensation trails ('contrails') that trap additional infrared heat—multiplying aviation's warming effect beyond CO2 alone.

Alarmed by soaring passenger numbers, climate campaigners urge governments to curb non-essential flights. Policy proposals include ending tax exemptions on jet kerosene, banning domestic routes already served by fast trains, and introducing a 'frequent-flyer levy'—a progressive tax that leaves one annual holiday flight untaxed while charging sharply higher fees on each additional journey. Research indicates that a tiny wealthy minority accounts for over half of all global passenger flights.

Aviation groups and hospitality associations push back firmly. They warn that steep ticket taxes could cripple the tourism industry in remote islands and developing economies where visitors arrive almost exclusively by air, threatening millions of jobs in hotels, restaurants, and local transport. Critics also argue that raising fares indiscriminately could erode travel freedom for working-class families visiting relatives abroad.

Rather than shrinking flight volumes, airlines heavily promote voluntary carbon offset schemes built on a three-stage verification model. First, booking software computes a passenger's flight footprint based on route distance and cabin class. Next, the traveller's payment buys certified carbon credits funding projects like forest preservation or clean cookstoves. Finally, external registries retire those credits permanently so they cannot be resold. Yet independent investigations have found that many offset schemes exaggerate their climate benefits, leading experts to argue that cutting unnecessary trips and scaling up sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) remain indispensable.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 2
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.
passages.title: Cleaner Cities: From Car-Free Days to Cycling
passages.subtitle: Reclaiming congested urban streets through vehicle-free zones, protected bike lanes, and integrated transit
paragraphs: 1 For much of the twentieth century, urban engineers tried to cure traffic congestion by widening boulevards and building multi-lane flyovers. Yet transport researchers consistently observe a counterintuitive phenomenon called 'induced demand': adding extra road space simply encourages more people to drive, quickly filling new lanes with gridlock and worsening urban air pollution. Today, forward-thinking mayors are reversing course by prioritising sustainable transport.

2 One widely copied catalyst for change is the regular car-free day. Inspired by Bogota's famous Ciclovia—which closes major arteries to private cars every Sunday—cities from Jakarta to Brussels now temporarily open central roads to pedestrians, skaters, and cyclists. Even when initially limited to a single day, vehicle-free events allow sceptical shopkeepers and residents to experience quieter air and brisk foot traffic firsthand.

3 Critics often dismiss annual car-free days as symbolic gestures that do little to alter weekday rush-hour patterns. Urban sociologists disagree, pointing out that cities frequently use temporary road closures as low-cost public trials. In Paris, temporary pedestrian zones along the River Seine proved so popular with families that city officials converted them permanently into riverside promenades and commuting routes.

4 Expanding everyday cycling delivers some of the highest health and carbon returns per dollar invested. Studies from Copenhagen and Dutch cities confirm that painted lines on busy roads do not attract nervous riders; what transforms a city's daily commute is physically separated cycle lanes, priority traffic signals, and secure weatherproof bike parking at rail hubs. When safety is built into street design, cycling shifts from a niche fitness hobby into an ordinary transport choice for children and seniors alike.

5 Nevertheless, planners acknowledge real constraints. Steep topography, monsoon downpours, scorching summer humidity, and long suburban distances make cycling impractical for many commuters. Likewise, people with mobility impairments, tradespeople hauling equipment, and parents transporting multiple toddlers cannot depend exclusively on bicycles.

6 Consequently, Europe's and Asia's cleanest metropolises treat cycling as one strand of an integrated network alongside frequent, affordable public transport. Pairing electric metro lines and dedicated bus lanes with shaded walkways and e-bike rentals ensures every resident can move efficiently without relying on a private petrol car.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Waste, Recycling and Plastic
passages.subtitle: Why voluntary recycling falls short—and how legislation, fines, and education can close the gap
paragraphs: 1 Global cities currently generate more than two billion tonnes of municipal solid waste annually—a volume projected to surge by seventy percent before 2050. Much of this rubbish is still buried in open or lined landfill sites, where decomposing organic scraps emit potent methane gas and rainfall carries toxic leachate toward groundwater. Managing waste is therefore both a local sanitation issue and an urgent climate challenge.

2 Two waste streams stand out for their scale and persistence: food waste and plastic. Roughly a third of global food production is lost or discarded, fuelled by strict cosmetic supermarket standards, oversized restaurant portions, and confused household shopping. Meanwhile, cheap single-use plastic—wrappers, sachets, and carrier bags—drives severe plastic pollution across waterways and oceans, breaking down into microplastics that enter marine food webs and even human bloodstreams.

3 For decades, governments and corporations promoted consumer recycling as the primary fix. Yet the global plastic recycling rate hovers stubbornly below ten percent. Complex multi-layer food pouches are technically impossible to separate, while greasy takeaway boxes routinely contaminate entire batches of otherwise clean paper. Even when sorted properly, recycled plastic struggles to compete economically whenever cheap crude oil makes virgin plastic resin inexpensive to manufacture.

4 Recognising the failure of purely voluntary habits, policymakers are turning to enforceable rules. Over ninety nations now enforce a partial or total ban on thin plastic bags, while France prohibits supermarkets from throwing away unsold edible groceries, requiring donations to charities instead. In South Korea, a 'pay-as-you-throw' system weighs household food scraps and charges fees accordingly, while municipal inspectors impose fines on residents and firms that mix recyclables with general rubbish—lifting South Korea's food recycling rate above ninety percent.

5 Increasingly, regulators are also adopting 'extended producer responsibility' (EPR) laws that make packaging manufacturers pay for collection and sorting costs—giving companies a financial incentive to simplify materials. Alongside legislation, early education remains vital. Schools in Japan and Taiwan integrate daily waste sorting and cafeteria zero-waste lunches into the curriculum, while public campaigns raise awareness about date labels so families distinguish safety deadlines from cosmetic 'best-before' guidelines.

6 Closing the global waste gap will never happen through recycling bins alone. Lasting progress requires combining upstream bans and producer accountability with fair household fines and school-based habits—shifting society from managing mountains of trash to preventing waste before it is ever created.
